table.note: A written standup posted in one channel works well across time zones.

sections.title: How to motivate a remote team
body: Motivation comes from the same places it does in an office, but remotely it has to be said out loud more often.

items.title: Recognise work in public
items.body: Thank people specifically, in the team channel, for what they did and why it mattered.

items.title: Give real ownership
items.body: Hand over whole problems, not just tasks. People care more about work they decided how to do.

items.title: Show where the work goes
items.body: Share customer feedback and results, so people see the effect of what they make.

items.title: Invest in growth
items.body: Ask what each person wants to learn, and give them work that stretches them.

items.title: Protect their time
items.body: Fewer meetings and quiet focus hours are a reward in themselves.

items.title: Monitoring software
items.body: Keystroke loggers and webcam checks tell people you don't trust them, and your best people are the first to leave.

items.title: Too many meetings
items.body: Video calls are more tiring than meeting in person. If a meeting could be a written update, make it one.

items.title: Everything in private messages
items.body: Work discussed in direct messages is invisible to everyone else. Default to team channels.

items.title: No onboarding plan
items.body: New remote hires can go weeks without knowing who to ask. Give them a buddy and a [plan for their first two weeks](/guides/remote-onboarding-checklist).

items.title: Ignoring time zones
items.body: Rotate meeting times, write down what you can, and never make the same people take every late call.

sections.title: Tools that help
body: You need fewer tools than you think: one each for chat, meetings, docs and tasks, plus a way to see who's around. Our [guide to remote work tools](/guides/remote-work-tools) goes through each job, with starter stacks for small teams.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor makes presence visible: a virtual office in the browser where your team sees who's around, who's in a meeting and who wants quiet, and walks over to talk. It brings back the hallway moments a remote team misses, without cameras left on or tracking. It's free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: How do you manage a remote team well?
faq.a: Write down how the team works, agree on overlap hours, keep a steady meeting rhythm with weekly one-to-ones, make work and people visible, and judge results rather than hours.

faq.q: How do you keep a remote team motivated?
faq.a: Recognise work in public, give people ownership, share the effect of their work, invest in their growth and make regular time to connect.

faq.q: How often should a remote team meet?
faq.a: A short daily standup (or a written one), a weekly team meeting, weekly or fortnightly one-to-ones and a retrospective every few weeks is enough for most small teams.

faq.q: Should you monitor remote employees?
faq.a: Activity tracking tends to damage trust without improving results. Agree on clear goals and check the outcomes instead.

faq.q: What is hardest about managing a remote team?
faq.a: Seeing problems early. Without a shared office you won't notice someone is stuck or struggling unless you make room for it, which is what one-to-ones and visible presence are for.

happyHour.label: Virtual happy hour ideas

meta.title: 20 Virtual Happy Hour Ideas Your Remote Team Will Actually Join
meta.description: 20 virtual happy hour ideas for remote teams: no-prep ideas, games, activities worth a little planning and ideas for big or spread-out teams, plus how to host one people enjoy.

happyHour.title: Virtual happy hour ideas people actually show up for.
happyHour.intro: Most virtual happy hours fail the same way: twenty people in one video call, two talking, everyone else waiting for it to end. The ones that work are short, optional and give people something to do, in groups small enough to talk. Here are 20 ideas, sorted by how much preparation they need, and how to host one.

sections.title: What makes a virtual happy hour work

items.title: Short
items.body: Thirty to forty-five minutes. People stay longer when they want to, and come back when it didn't drag.

items.title: Optional
items.body: Inside working hours, and truly optional. A happy hour people must attend is a meeting.

items.title: Something to do
items.body: A game, a question or a theme gives quieter people an easy way in.

items.title: Small groups
items.body: More than six or seven people in one conversation, and most of them stop talking. Split up.

items.title: Not about drinks
items.body: Coffee, tea or a soft drink is just as welcome. Call it a social if the name puts people off.

sections.title: No-prep ideas
body: Start here. Each of these works with five minutes' notice.

items.title: Show and tell
items.body: Everyone shows one thing within reach and tells its story. A mug, a book, a plant, a pet that wandered in.

items.title: Two truths and a lie
items.body: Each person says three things about themselves; the others guess the lie. Our [two truths and a lie ideas](/tools/two-truths-and-a-lie) help anyone stuck for something to say.

items.title: Would you rather
items.body: Read out a question, let everyone answer and defend their choice. Our [would you rather questions](/tools/would-you-rather-questions) are sorted for work.

items.title: Desk tour
items.body: Turn the camera round for thirty seconds each. It's surprising how much people learn about each other from a bookshelf.

items.title: Photo of the week
items.body: Each person shares one photo from their week and says why they took it.

items.title: Question round
items.body: One light question, everyone answers: best meal this year, first concert, a skill they'd like to learn. Pick from our [icebreaker questions](/tools/icebreaker-questions).

sections.title: Games
body: Games give a happy hour a shape, so nobody has to think of what to say next.

items.title: Trivia
items.detail: Teams of 3 to 5 · 15 minutes to prepare
items.body: Five rounds of five questions, one round about the company. Rotate who writes the questions each month.

items.title: Draw and guess
items.body: One person draws a word on a shared whiteboard, the rest guess. Free browser games such as skribbl.io run the rounds for you.

items.title: Baby photo guess
items.body: Collect a childhood photo from each person beforehand, then show them one by one and guess who's who.

items.title: Team bingo
items.body: Bingo cards of facts about the team: "has lived in three countries", "plays an instrument". People ask each other to fill the squares.

items.title: Word and party games online
items.body: Codenames, Gartic Phone and similar browser games need only a link, and most are free.

sections.title: Ideas worth a little planning
body: Keep these for once a month or a special occasion; a bit of preparation makes them feel like an event.

items.title: Tasting
items.detail: Any size · order a week ahead
items.body: Send everyone the same coffee, tea, chocolate or snacks, then taste and rate them together.

items.title: Cook or mix along
items.detail: Up to 12 · share a list ahead
items.body: One person who loves cooking leads a simple recipe or a drink, with or without alcohol.

items.title: Lightning talks
items.detail: Up to 15 · a few days' notice
items.body: Three volunteers each talk for five minutes about anything but work: a hobby, a trip, how to make bread.

items.title: Playlist party
items.body: Everyone adds two songs to a shared playlist; play them and guess who picked what.

items.title: Online escape room
items.body: Hosted escape rooms run over video and suit teams that like puzzles. Most charge per person.

sections.title: Ideas for big or spread-out teams
body: Above fifteen people, or across many time zones, one shared call stops working. Mix small groups and written formats.

items.title: Rotating small groups
items.body: Groups of four for ten minutes, then reshuffle. In a virtual office people simply walk from one group to another, as at a real party.

items.title: Random coffee pairs
items.body: Pair people at random for a fifteen-minute chat at a time that suits them both. Over a few months everyone meets everyone.

items.title: A happy hour that moves with the sun
items.body: Hold it twice, at a time that suits each half of the team, or start a photo thread that runs all day.

items.title: Seasonal theme
items.detail: Any size · a few days' notice
items.body: Hats in winter, favourite snacks from home, a fancy-dress Friday. A theme gives people something to talk about before anyone speaks.

items.title: Pick a time inside working hours
items.body: Late afternoon on a Thursday or Friday works for many teams. Across time zones, use our [time zone meeting planner](/tools/time-zone-meeting-planner) to find the overlap.

items.title: Invite with a plan
items.body: "30 minutes, two rounds of trivia, then chat" gets more people than "happy hour, 5pm".

items.title: Open with one easy question
items.body: Everyone answers in a sentence. It gets every voice in the room in the first five minutes.

items.title: Split groups above six
items.body: Use breakout rooms, or a space where people can drift between groups on their own.

items.title: End on time
items.body: Close at the time you said. Anyone who wants to stay can, but nobody feels trapped.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: On TinyFloor a happy hour feels more like a room than a call. Everyone walks onto the same floor, small groups form where people stand, and you join a conversation by walking over, so nobody is stuck in one twenty-person grid. A whiteboard for drawing games is on the wall. It's free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: What do you do at a virtual happy hour?
faq.a: Talk in small groups and do something light together: a question round, a game such as trivia or draw and guess, show and tell or a tasting.

faq.q: How long should a virtual happy hour be?
faq.a: Thirty to forty-five minutes is enough for most teams. Shorter and people don't settle in; longer and the energy drops.

faq.q: How do you make a virtual happy hour fun?
faq.a: Keep it optional, give it a plan, start with an easy question for everyone and split into groups of four to six so everyone talks.

faq.q: Does a virtual happy hour need alcohol?
faq.a: No. Make it clear that any drink is fine, and consider calling it a social. Many of the best ideas have nothing to do with drinks.

faq.q: How often should a remote team have a happy hour?
faq.a: Once a month suits most teams. A short weekly social works too, if it stays optional and short.

oneOnOne.label: One-on-one meeting questions

meta.title: One-on-One Meeting Template and 40 Questions for Managers
meta.description: 40 one-on-one meeting questions sorted by topic: check-ins, workload, blockers, feedback, growth, the team and remote work, plus questions to ask your manager and a simple 1:1 agenda.

oneOnOne.title: One-on-one meeting questions that get real answers.
oneOnOne.intro: A one-on-one is the one meeting that belongs to the other person. It's where a manager hears about problems early, and on a remote team, often the only place they will. Here are 40 questions, sorted by topic, a simple agenda, and how to keep the meeting from turning into a status update.

sections.title: How to run a good one-on-one

items.title: It's their meeting
items.body: Let them bring topics first. Your topics come after.

items.title: Not a status update
items.body: Status belongs on the task board. Use the time for the person: how they feel, what's in the way, where they want to go.

items.title: Same time, every week or two
items.body: Thirty minutes, rarely moved. Cancelling often tells people they come last.

items.title: One shared document
items.body: Both add topics during the week and note what you agreed, so nothing is lost between meetings.

items.title: A few questions, followed up
items.body: Two good questions and a real follow-up beat ten read from a list.

head: Part
Time
What happens
rows: How they are, in their own words
What each of you will do before next time
table.note: Thirty minutes in all. If their topics run long, move yours to next time.

items.title: How are you, really?
items.body: The "really" invites more than "fine". Wait for the answer.

items.title: What's been on your mind this week?
items.body: Open enough to bring up anything, work or not.

items.title: What was the best part of your week?
items.body: Starts on something good and shows what energises them.

items.title: What drained your energy this week?
items.body: Points to the work, meetings or people that wear them down.

items.title: On a scale of one to ten, how was your week?
items.body: A quick number makes changes easy to spot over a few weeks.

items.title: Is your workload too much, too little or about right?
items.body: Ask it plainly; people rarely volunteer that they're overloaded.

items.title: What are you working on that you think matters most?
items.body: Checks that their priorities match yours.

items.title: Is there anything you're working on that feels pointless?
items.body: Often finds work that can simply stop.

items.title: What would you drop if you had to?
items.body: Shows what they value, and what they'd quietly like to hand off.

items.title: Do you have enough focus time?
items.body: [Too many meetings](/guides/async-communication) is one of the most common remote complaints.

items.title: What's slowing you down right now?
items.body: The most useful question a manager can ask, and the most often skipped.

items.title: Is there a decision you're waiting on?
items.body: Waiting on someone else is invisible until you ask.

items.title: What's one thing I could do to make your work easier?
items.body: Gives them permission to ask for help.

items.title: Is anything frustrating you that you haven't mentioned?
items.body: Small frustrations grow when they go unsaid.

items.title: Who do you find it hard to work with, and why?
items.body: Ask carefully; it surfaces friction before it becomes conflict.

items.title: What's one thing I should do differently as your manager?
items.body: Ask it regularly and react calmly, or the answers stop.

items.title: Is there anything I do that gets in your way?
items.body: A gentler form of the same question.

items.title: How do you like to receive feedback?
items.body: Some want it written, some in the moment, some saved for the one-on-one.

items.title: What are you proudest of from the last month?
items.body: Gives you something specific to recognise.

items.title: Is there feedback you'd like that you're not getting?
items.body: People often want more feedback than managers think.

items.title: What would you like to be doing in a year?
items.body: Starts a career conversation without asking for a five-year plan.

items.title: What skill would you like to get better at?
items.body: Lets you look for work that builds it.

items.title: What part of your work do you enjoy most?
items.body: More of it is often the cheapest reward there is.

items.title: Is there a project you'd love to be part of?
items.body: Interest is half of what makes someone good at something new.

items.title: Who would you like to learn from?
items.body: A mentor or [pairing](/remote-pair-programming) can do more than a course.

items.title: How do you feel about the team right now?
items.body: Picks up on tension before anyone names it.

items.title: Is there anything about how we work that you'd change?
items.body: People who do the work see what's broken first.

items.title: Do you understand why we're doing what we're doing?
items.body: If not, the problem is the explanation, not the person.

items.title: Who on the team deserves more credit?
items.body: A good way to hear about quiet work.

items.title: Is there anything you've heard that worries you?
items.body: Rumours travel fast on remote teams and are rarely said out loud.

items.title: Do you feel connected to the team?
items.body: Isolation is the most common remote problem, and the least likely to be raised.

items.title: Do you know who to ask when you're stuck?
items.body: If not, they're probably waiting quietly.

items.title: Are your working hours working for you?
items.body: Covers [time zones](/tools/time-zone-meeting-planner), late calls and the line between work and home.

items.title: Is your home setup slowing you down?
items.body: A chair, a screen or better internet is a cheap fix.

items.title: Are there too many meetings, or too few?
items.body: Remote teams drift into both.

sections.title: Questions to ask your manager
body: One-on-ones go both ways. If you're the one being managed, these help you get more from the meeting.

items.title: What should I focus on most right now?
items.body: Makes sure your effort goes where it counts.

items.title: What would make my work more useful to you?
items.body: Shows what they need, not just what they ask for.

items.title: What's one thing I could do better?
items.body: Ask for one thing; it's easier to answer honestly.

items.title: What's coming up for the team that I should know about?
items.body: Context you'd otherwise hear last.

items.title: What would I need to show to take on more?
items.body: Turns a vague wish to grow into something concrete.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: On TinyFloor a one-on-one doesn't need a calendar link: walk into a meeting room together, or step aside on the floor and talk. Between one-on-ones, you can see who's around, so a quick check-in doesn't have to wait a week. It's free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: What should you talk about in a one-on-one?
faq.a: The person, not the status: how they are, what's in their way, feedback in both directions and where they want to grow.

faq.q: How often should you have one-on-ones?
faq.a: Weekly or every two weeks, for about thirty minutes. Weekly suits new team members and remote teams best.

faq.q: What are good one-on-one questions for employees to ask?
faq.a: What should I focus on most, what would make my work more useful, what could I do better, and what's coming up that I should know about.

faq.q: How do you start a one-on-one?
faq.a: With an open check-in question such as "How are you, really?", then let them bring their topics before yours.

faq.q: What should a manager avoid in a one-on-one?
faq.a: Turning it into a status update, talking more than listening, and cancelling or moving it often.

async.label: Async communication

meta.title: Async Communication: What It Is and How Remote Teams Do It Well
meta.description: What async communication is, how it differs from sync, when to use each, how to write messages that work without a reply, rituals and tools, and the problems to watch for.

async.title: Async communication, and when to stop and talk.
async.intro: Async communication means sending a message without expecting an answer right away: the other person replies when it suits them. It lets remote teams work across time zones and protect focus time. It also makes simple things slow when it's used for everything. Here's how to use it well, and when to switch to a conversation instead.

sections.title: What async communication is
body: Synchronous (sync) communication happens live: a call, a meeting, a chat at someone's desk. Asynchronous (async) communication doesn't: a message, a document, a comment or a recorded video that people read or watch later.
Most remote teams use both. The skill is choosing the right one for each conversation, and writing async messages that don't need three rounds of questions to understand.

head: Sync
Async
rows: Updates, questions that can wait, decisions that need thought

items.title: Updates
items.body: Status, progress and what's next. A [written standup](/tools/daily-standup-template) replaces most daily calls.

items.title: Questions that can wait
items.body: If the answer can come this afternoon, send a message.

items.title: Decisions that need thought
items.body: Write the proposal down and give people a day to comment. You'll get better input than in a meeting.

items.title: Anything across time zones
items.body: When the team's hours barely overlap, async is the default and live time is for what needs it.

items.title: A thread has gone back and forth three times
items.body: Two minutes of talking will settle it. Write down what you decided afterwards.

items.title: Someone is blocked
items.body: Unblocking a teammate is worth an interruption.

items.title: The topic is sensitive
items.body: Feedback, conflict and bad news land better in a conversation, where tone comes through.

items.title: You're starting something new
items.body: Kickoffs and brainstorms move faster when people can build on each other's ideas live.

sections.title: How to write async messages that work

items.title: Lead with the point
items.body: Put the question or the decision in the first line, then the background.

items.title: Give all the context
items.body: Links, screenshots and what you've already tried, so nobody has to ask.

items.title: Say what you need, and by when
items.body: "Can you review this by Thursday?" gets an answer; "thoughts?" often doesn't.

items.title: One message, not five
items.body: Write it in full before sending. A stream of short messages interrupts people five times.

items.title: Use threads
items.body: Keep replies with the message they answer, so the channel stays readable.

items.title: Write the decision down
items.body: When a thread ends, post the outcome in one line where people will find it.

items.title: A written daily standup
items.body: Yesterday, today and anything blocking, posted in one channel at any time in each person's morning.

items.title: A weekly update
items.body: Each person or team writes a few lines on progress, problems and plans. Easy to skim on Monday.

items.title: Decision documents
items.body: A short page per important decision: the problem, the options, the choice and why.

items.title: Recorded demos
items.body: A few minutes of screen recording shows a feature better than a meeting, and people watch it when it suits them.

sections.title: Agree on response times
body: Async only works when everyone knows how long "later" is. Write it down in your team handbook.

head: Channel
Expected reply
Use it for
rows: Comment on a doc or task
table.note: An example, not a rule: pick times that fit your team, and say what counts as urgent.

items.title: Decisions crawl
items.body: Set a deadline for comments, and give one person the final say.

items.title: Too much to read
items.body: Fewer channels, shorter messages and a weekly summary help more than reading faster.

items.title: People feel cut off
items.body: All-async teams can feel lonely. Keep some live time: a weekly meeting, a social, or a shared space to see who's around. Our guide to [remote team communication](/guides/remote-team-communication) covers the balance.

items.title: Urgent things wait
items.body: Agree on one clear way to reach someone right away, and keep it for what's really urgent.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor is the sync half that async teams miss. Your chat, docs and recordings stay where they are; when a thread stalls, you can see who's around on the floor and walk over to talk for two minutes. Statuses show who's focused, so live conversations don't cost anyone their deep work. It's free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: What is async communication?
faq.a: Communication where people don't reply right away: messages, documents, comments and recorded videos that others read or watch when it suits them.

faq.q: What's the difference between sync and async communication?
faq.a: Sync happens live, like a call or a meeting, and gets an answer right away. Async doesn't need everyone at once, and answers come later.

faq.q: What are examples of async communication?
faq.a: A chat message, an email, a comment on a document, a written standup, a weekly update or a recorded video demo.

faq.q: Is async communication better for remote teams?
faq.a: For updates, questions that can wait and teams across time zones, yes. For urgent, sensitive or tangled topics, a live conversation is usually better. Most teams need both.

faq.q: What tools are used for async communication?
faq.a: Team chat with threads, shared documents, task boards and screen recording tools. Our guide to remote work tools covers each.

retro.label: Retrospective ideas

meta.title: 15 Retrospective Ideas and a Template for Remote Teams
meta.description: 15 retrospective ideas for remote teams: quick formats, visual formats, deeper formats and ones that lift the mood, with how to run a retro online and keep the actions moving.

retro.title: Retrospective ideas for teams that are tired of the same three questions.
retro.intro: A retrospective is a short meeting where a team looks back on a stretch of work and agrees what to change. It's one of the most useful habits a team can have, and one of the easiest to let go stale. Here are 15 formats to keep retros fresh, how to run one online, and how to make sure something actually changes afterwards.

sections.title: How a retro runs
body: Whatever the format, most good retros follow the same five steps. The formats below change the middle; keep the start and the end.

head: Step
Time
What happens
rows: A quick check-in, and a reminder that it's about the work, not blame
Everyone writes notes on their own, then shares
Group the notes and vote on what matters most
Two or three concrete changes, each with an owner
Check last time's actions, and a one-line round on the retro itself
table.note: Forty-five minutes suits a team of up to ten, every two to four weeks.

sections.title: Quick formats
body: For short retros, or a team new to them.

items.title: Start, stop, continue
items.body: What should we start doing, stop doing and keep doing? Simple and always useful.

items.title: Mad, sad, glad
items.body: What made people angry, disappointed or pleased. Good after a hard stretch.

items.title: Keep, add, less, more
items.body: Four columns that let people suggest turning something up or down rather than on or off.

items.title: One word
items.body: Each person describes the last sprint in one word, then explains it. A good opener, or a whole retro on a busy week.

sections.title: Visual formats
body: Pictures make people think differently. Draw the frame on a shared whiteboard and let everyone add notes.

items.title: Sailboat
items.body: The island is the goal; wind is what pushed us forward, anchors held us back, rocks are risks ahead.

items.title: Rose, thorn, bud
items.body: A rose is something that went well, a thorn a problem, a bud an idea or opportunity starting to grow.

items.title: Starfish
items.body: Keep doing, less of, more of, stop doing, start doing. Useful when start, stop, continue feels too blunt.

items.title: Timeline
items.body: Draw the period as a line and let everyone mark highs and lows. Patterns show up that a list hides.

sections.title: Deeper formats
body: For when a problem keeps coming back, or a project has ended.

items.title: Five whys
items.body: Pick one problem and ask "why?" until you reach a cause you can change.

items.title: Pre-mortem
items.body: Imagine the next project has failed. What went wrong? Then plan to prevent the likeliest causes.

items.title: Lean coffee
items.body: Everyone suggests topics, the team votes, and you discuss them in order with a timer.

items.title: Liked, learned, lacked, longed for
items.body: Four questions that balance what went well with what was missing.

sections.title: Formats that lift the mood
body: After a tough release or a long quarter, start with what went right.

items.title: Kudos round
items.body: Everyone thanks someone for something specific. Then move on to what to change.

items.title: Three little pigs
items.body: What's fragile, what holds but could be stronger, and what's solid. Light-hearted, but it finds real risks.

items.title: Hopes and worries
items.body: What people hope for and what worries them about what's next. Pair it with a few [team building questions](/tools/team-building-questions) if the team is new.

items.title: Write first, in silence
items.body: Five minutes of everyone writing notes on their own gets ideas from quiet people, not just the loudest.

items.title: Use a shared board
items.body: A shared [online whiteboard](/online-whiteboard) or a simple doc with columns. Keep the same board from retro to retro so you can look back.

items.title: Keep cameras optional, voices on
items.body: What matters is that people talk; nobody needs to stare at a grid of faces for forty-five minutes.

items.title: Rotate the facilitator
items.body: Someone different each time keeps the format fresh and lets the manager just take part.

items.title: Allow anonymous notes when trust is low
items.body: Honest input beats polite input. Move back to named notes as trust grows.

items.title: Two or three actions, no more
items.body: A long list of actions means none of them happen.

items.title: An owner for each
items.body: "We should" isn't an action. A name and a date are.

items.title: Put them on the board
items.body: Add the actions to your task board with the rest of the work, not in a separate document.

items.title: Open with last time's actions
items.body: Start each retro by checking what happened to the last ones. It's the fastest way to show retros matter.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: On TinyFloor the retro happens where the team already is. Walk into the meeting room together, draw the sailboat on the whiteboard on the wall, and leave it up for next time. It's free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: What is a retrospective?
faq.a: A short, regular meeting where a team looks back on a stretch of work, talks about what went well and what didn't, and agrees on a few changes.

faq.q: How do you make a retrospective fun?
faq.a: Change the format every few retros, use visual formats such as the sailboat, open with kudos, and make sure the actions actually happen, so the time feels worth it.

faq.q: How long should a retrospective be?
faq.a: About forty-five minutes for a two-week sprint and a team of up to ten. Longer projects or bigger teams may need an hour.

faq.q: How often should a team hold a retrospective?
faq.a: At the end of each sprint, or every two to four weeks, plus one at the end of any big project.

faq.q: How do you run a retrospective remotely?
faq.a: Use a shared board, give people a few minutes to write on their own before discussing, keep it to a few actions with owners, and rotate who facilitates.

onboardingChecklist.label: Remote onboarding checklist

meta.title: Remote Onboarding Checklist: From Before Day One to Day 90
meta.description: A remote onboarding checklist for managers: what to do before day one, on the first day, in the first week and the first 90 days, who owns each step, and the mistakes to avoid.

onboardingChecklist.title: A remote onboarding checklist, from before day one to day 90.
onboardingChecklist.intro: Starting a new job remotely is lonely in a way an office isn't: no one to sit next to, no sense of who's around, and every question feels like an interruption. A good checklist fixes most of that. Here's what to do before day one, on the first day, and through the first three months, and who should own each step.

sections.title: Who owns what
body: [Onboarding](/remote-onboarding) goes wrong when everyone assumes someone else is doing it. Name an owner for each part.

head: Who
Owns
rows: The plan, goals for the first 90 days, weekly one-to-ones
Everyday questions, introductions, how things really work
Asking questions, writing down what was confusing, a first small piece of work

items.title: Send the equipment
items.body: Laptop and anything else they need, timed to arrive a few days early.

items.title: Create every account
items.body: Email, chat, docs, the task board and anything role-specific, tested before they log in.

items.title: Pick a buddy
items.body: A teammate who isn't their manager, with time set aside for the first two weeks.

items.title: Write the first-week plan
items.body: Who they'll meet, what they'll read and a first small task, shared before they start.

items.title: Tell the team
items.body: A short introduction in the team channel, so people say hello on day one.

items.title: Send a welcome message
items.body: Start time, first meeting and who to contact if anything doesn't work.

items.title: Start with a call with the manager
items.body: Welcome, the plan for the week and what good looks like in the first month.

items.title: Check every login works
items.body: Nothing kills a first day like an afternoon waiting on access.

items.title: Meet the buddy
items.body: A first chat, and an agreement to talk at least once a day for the first week.

items.title: A team welcome
items.body: A short, informal call or gathering. A light [icebreaker question](/tools/icebreaker-questions) helps everyone say something.

items.title: Point them to the handbook
items.body: How the team works, where to ask what, and where decisions live.

items.title: End the day with a check-in
items.body: Five minutes: how was it, and what's still unclear?

items.title: One-to-one intros
items.body: Fifteen minutes with each person they'll work with most.

items.title: Shadow real work
items.body: Sit in on calls, reviews and planning, with the buddy explaining what's going on.

items.title: Ship something small
items.body: A first task they can finish this week. Finishing something early builds confidence.

items.title: Agree on working hours
items.body: When they're online, the team's [overlap hours](/guides/how-to-manage-a-remote-team) and how fast people usually reply.

items.title: First weekly one-to-one
items.body: What's going well, what's confusing, and what they need.

items.title: 30 days: settled in
items.body: Knows the tools, the people and how work flows. Owns small pieces of work on their own.

items.title: 60 days: contributing
items.body: Takes on bigger work with less guidance and starts to spot what could be better.

items.title: 90 days: fully part of the team
items.body: Works independently, helps others, and has had a proper review of how onboarding went.

items.title: Ask what to fix
items.body: At 30 and 90 days, ask what was confusing or missing, and update the checklist for the next person.

items.title: A week of reading
items.body: Documents matter, but people learn faster by doing real work with someone beside them.

items.title: No one to ask
items.body: Without a buddy, new people sit on questions for hours rather than interrupt.

items.title: Invisible teammates
items.body: When you can't see who's around, it's hard to know when it's fine to ask. Make [presence visible](/team-presence).

items.title: Too many meetings at once
items.body: Spread the introductions over the first two weeks rather than ten calls on day one.

items.title: Onboarding stops after week one
items.body: The first three months shape whether people stay. Keep the [one-to-ones](/guides/one-on-one-meeting-questions) and the check-ins going.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: On TinyFloor a new hire can see the whole team on one floor from day one: who's around, who's in a meeting and who's free. Asking a question is a short walk, not a booked call, and the buddy is a few desks away. It's free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: What should a remote onboarding checklist include?
faq.a: Equipment and accounts before day one, a buddy, a first-week plan, introductions, a small first task, weekly one-to-ones and goals for 30, 60 and 90 days.

faq.q: How long should remote onboarding take?
faq.a: Most people need about three months to be fully settled, with the most support in the first two weeks.

faq.q: How do you make remote employees feel welcome?
faq.a: Have everything ready on day one, give them a buddy, introduce them to the team early and check in every day in the first week.

faq.q: What is an onboarding buddy?
faq.a: A teammate, not the manager, who answers everyday questions and makes introductions during a new hire's first weeks.

faq.q: What's the hardest part of remote onboarding?
faq.a: Knowing who to ask and when it's fine to interrupt. A buddy and visible presence fix most of it.

bodyDoubling.label: Body doubling

meta.title: Body Doubling: What It Is, the Apps, and How to Do It Online
meta.description: What body doubling is, why working next to someone makes it easier to start and keep going, the ways to do it online, how to run a session and how to body double with your own team.

bodyDoubling.title: Body doubling: work next to someone, get more done.
bodyDoubling.intro: Body doubling means working with another person nearby, in the same room or on a screen, so it's easier to start a task and stay on it. The other person isn't helping with the work; they're just there. Many people with ADHD describe it as one of the few things that reliably works, and plenty of remote workers use it to replace the quiet company of an office. Here's what it is, the ways to do it online and how to run a session that works.

sections.title: What body doubling is
body: A body double is someone who works alongside you while you do a task you'd otherwise put off: paperwork, a report, studying, cleaning, a hard email. They can be doing their own work, or just reading. What matters is that someone is there.

The idea comes from ADHD coaching, and the name has spread well beyond it. Students use it to study, freelancers to get through admin, and remote teams to keep the feeling of working in a room together.

sections.title: Why it seems to help
body: Research on body doubling itself is still thin; most of what's known comes from people's own experience. The reasons people give are consistent, though.

items.title: Starting is easier
items.body: Saying out loud what you're about to do, to someone who's sitting down to work too, makes it harder to put off.

items.title: Gentle accountability
items.body: Nobody checks your work, but knowing someone will ask "how did it go?" at the end is often enough.

items.title: Fewer drifts
items.body: With someone there, reaching for the phone or opening another tab feels more noticeable, so it happens less.

items.title: Less lonely
items.body: For people [working from home](/virtual-office), the quiet company of another person makes long stretches of work feel lighter.

head: Way
Who's there
Good for
rows: A video call with a friend
Free and simple; agree a time and keep cameras on or off
A stranger, booked for a timed session
When nobody you know is free, and you like a fixed slot
Group sessions, such as Flow Club
A host and a group, at set times
Structure and company, with people who show up to work
A quick start when no one is around; no accountability
Your teammates or a small group
All-day company with people you know, talking when you need
table.note: Each suits a different need. Many people mix them: a friend for hard tasks, a recording for small ones.

sections.title: How to run a body doubling session

items.title: Agree a time and a length
items.body: Fifty minutes of work is a common choice; start with 25 if a task feels heavy.

items.title: Say what you'll do
items.body: One sentence each: the task and what done looks like. Specific beats ambitious.

items.title: Work quietly
items.body: Microphones off, cameras up to you. Resist chatting; the point is the work.

items.title: Check in at the end
items.body: One sentence each again: done, not done, what's next. No judgement either way.

items.title: Take a short break
items.body: Five or ten minutes, then start another session or call it a day.

head: Part
Time
What happens
table.note: Repeat as many times as suits the day. Keep the same start time to make it a habit.

items.title: Same time, every day
items.body: A standing slot removes the decision about whether to start.

items.title: Cameras are optional
items.body: Some people need to be seen, others find it distracting. Agree what suits everyone.

items.title: Keep tasks small
items.body: "Write the first page" works better than "write the report".

items.title: Don't turn it into a meeting
items.body: If the session becomes a chat, the work doesn't happen. Talk at the check-in and the break.

items.title: Be kind about bad sessions
items.body: Some days nothing gets done. Saying so at the check-out, without excuses, is part of what keeps people coming back.

sections.title: Body doubling with your team
body: Remote teams can body double without any extra app: the team is already there. In a shared [virtual coworking space](/virtual-coworking) everyone can [see who's working](/team-presence), sit at their own desk and set themselves busy, so a quiet afternoon still feels shared.

For more structure, start a [meeting](/virtual-meeting-room) called Focus, ask in whoever wants to join, and run the session plan above. People who'd rather not talk can simply be on the floor, working near everyone else.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor is a private virtual office for people who know each other: a small team, a few friends, a study group. Sit at your desks, set yourself busy, start a focus session in the meeting room, and talk when you need to. It's free for up to 3 people, so two friends can body double there at no cost. It doesn't match you with strangers.

faq.q: What is body doubling?
faq.a: Working with another person nearby, in person or online, to make it easier to start a task and keep going. The other person doesn't help with the work; they're just there.

faq.q: What is the best body doubling app?
faq.a: It depends on who you want there. Focusmate pairs you with a stranger for a timed session, group apps such as Flow Club run hosted sessions, and a virtual office such as TinyFloor puts you next to people you already know, all day. A video call with a friend works too, and costs nothing.

faq.q: Is body doubling only for ADHD?
faq.a: No. The term comes from ADHD coaching and many people with ADHD find it useful, but students, freelancers and remote workers use it too.

faq.q: Does body doubling need video?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Some people need to be seen; others only need to know someone is working too. Voice, a shared virtual office or cameras on all work.

faq.q: How long should a body doubling session be?
faq.a: Around 50 minutes of work with a short check-in and check-out is common. Start with 25 minutes if a task feels hard to begin.

faq.q: Can I body double for free?
faq.a: Yes. A video call with a friend costs nothing, and TinyFloor is free for up to 3 people, so a small group can body double there every day.

teamMeetingAgenda.label: Team meeting agenda

meta.title: Team Meeting Agenda Template: A Weekly Meeting That Works
meta.description: A weekly team meeting agenda template you can copy, what belongs in it and what doesn't, ideas to keep it fresh, and how to run it with a remote team in 30 minutes.

teamMeetingAgenda.title: A team meeting agenda that's worth the half hour.
teamMeetingAgenda.intro: A weekly team meeting is the one time everyone is in the same room, so it should do what written updates can't: decide things, unblock people and keep the team feeling like a team. Here's a 30-minute agenda template you can copy, what to put in it, what to take out, and how to run it when the team is remote.

sections.title: What a team meeting is for
body: Status updates are the most common item on a team meeting agenda and the least useful one. Everyone reading out what they did is slow, and most of it could have been a message.

Keep the meeting for what needs people together: decisions that affect several people, problems someone is stuck on, priorities for the week, and a few minutes that are just about the team. Everything else can be written down before or after.

sections.title: A weekly team meeting agenda template
body: Copy this into your calendar invite or your team's notes. The times are for a team of 5 to 10; a larger team needs more time for decisions, not more updates.

head: Part
Time
What happens
rows: One question everyone answers in a sentence
Something shipped, solved or learned since last week
The two or three figures the team watches, and whether they moved
What matters most this week, and who owns it
Items people added beforehand, in order
Decisions, owners and deadlines, read back
table.note: 30 minutes in all. If there's nothing under blockers and decisions, end early.

items.title: A shared list before the meeting
items.body: Anyone can add an item during the week, with their name and what they need: a decision, advice, or just to share. The meeting works through the list in order.

items.title: Decisions, written as questions
items.body: "Do we move the launch to Thursday?" gets decided. "Launch" gets discussed for ten minutes and ends with no answer.

items.title: One number per area
items.body: Sign-ups, open bugs, hours to first reply: whatever the team actually steers by. Say whether it moved; save the story behind it for when it matters.

items.title: Who's away
items.body: Holidays, half-days and launches coming up, so nobody waits on someone who isn't there.

items.title: Thanks
items.body: A minute for naming who helped whom. It costs nothing and it's often the part people remember.

items.title: Round-the-table updates
items.body: Ask for them in writing the day before. The meeting can then spend its time on the two updates that raised a question.

items.title: Long debates
items.body: If an item takes more than ten minutes, it needs its own smaller meeting with the people it affects.

items.title: Announcements
items.body: Post them in the [team chat](/team-chat), where people can read them later and react.

items.title: Things only two people care about
items.body: Let them talk after the meeting, or straight away if they're sitting near each other.

items.title: Rotate who runs it
items.body: A different person each week keeps the time and the list. It spreads the habit of running a good meeting.

items.title: A five-minute demo
items.body: Once a month, someone shows what they built or found, live, with no slides.

items.title: A better check-in question
items.body: "How was your weekend?" gets the same answers every week. Use a [question that tells the team something new](/guides/check-in-questions).

items.title: A game now and then
items.body: A five-minute [game](/guides/games-for-virtual-meetings) at the start, once a month, is enough to change the mood without taking over the meeting.

items.title: Skip a week
items.body: If the list is empty, cancel it. Nobody minds getting half an hour back, and the next one gets more attention.

sections.title: Running it with a remote team
body: On a call, the meeting starts with a link someone has to find and ends with everyone vanishing. In a virtual office, the team walks into the same [meeting room](/virtual-meeting-room) at the same time, and the people who need to keep talking afterwards can stay at their desks next to each other.

Keep cameras optional, share the agenda on screen so everyone is looking at the same item, and put the notes in the team chat before the room empties. If the team spans time zones, rotate the time so the same people aren't always on at night.

items.title: Post the notes
items.body: [Decisions, owners and deadlines](/guides/meeting-minutes-template), in the team chat, within the hour.

items.title: Move the open items
items.body: Anything not reached goes to the top of next week's list, or to its own meeting.

items.title: Tell the people who missed it
items.body: One line each on what affects them, so nobody learns about a decision by accident.

items.title: Check the time
items.body: If the meeting ran over two weeks in a row, cut an item from the template rather than adding time.

items.title: Kickoff meeting
items.body: Why the project exists (5 minutes), what done looks like (10), who owns what (10), the first milestones and dates (10), risks and open questions (10), and how the team will keep in touch (5). An hour in all, once per project.

items.title: All-hands meeting
items.body: Wins and thanks (10 minutes), the numbers that matter (10), what changed and why (15), one team showing its work (10), and questions from anyone (15). An hour, monthly or quarterly, with questions collected beforehand so quieter people get theirs in.

items.title: Daily standup
items.body: Ten to fifteen minutes: what each person is on today and anything blocking them. Our [daily standup template](/tools/daily-standup-template) has the questions and a written version for teams across time zones.

items.title: Retrospective
items.body: What went well, what didn't and what to change, every two to four weeks. See [retrospective ideas](/guides/retrospective-ideas) for formats that keep it fresh.

items.title: One-on-one
items.body: Thirty minutes between a manager and one person, led by their list rather than the manager's. Use our [one-on-one template and questions](/guides/one-on-one-meeting-questions).

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor is a virtual office for small teams. The weekly meeting happens in the meeting room everyone walks into, with video, screen sharing and a whiteboard, and afterwards people are back at their desks on the same floor, a short walk away if something needs a follow-up. It's free for up to 3 people and $29 a month for the whole team.

faq.q: What should be on a team meeting agenda?
faq.a: A short check-in, wins, the few numbers the team watches, this week's priorities, blockers and decisions that people added beforehand, and a wrap-up with owners and deadlines. Leave routine status updates for writing.

faq.q: How long should a weekly team meeting be?
faq.a: About 30 minutes for a team of 5 to 10. If it keeps running over, the problem is usually too many updates or a debate that needs its own meeting.

faq.q: How do you make team meetings less boring?
faq.a: Cut the updates, rotate who runs it, use a check-in question that tells the team something new, and show real work now and then. A meeting that ends early when there's nothing to decide is rarely called boring.

faq.q: Who should run the team meeting?
faq.a: Not always the manager. Rotating it keeps people engaged and teaches everyone to keep time and steer a discussion.

faq.q: Should the agenda be shared before the meeting?
faq.a: Yes. A shared list that anyone can add to during the week means the meeting starts with what people actually need, in order.

faq.q: What should a kickoff meeting agenda include?
faq.a: Why the project exists, what done looks like, who owns what, the first milestones, risks and open questions, and how the team will stay in touch. About an hour, once at the start.

discordVsSlack.label: Discord vs Slack

meta.title: Discord vs Slack for Work: Which Should a Small Team Use?
meta.description: Discord vs Slack for a work team: what each costs, voice and calls, message history, integrations and privacy, which suits a small team, and a third option built as an office.

discordVsSlack.title: Discord vs Slack for a work team.
discordVsSlack.intro: Plenty of small teams run their day in Discord: it's free, voice channels feel like a shared room, and many people already have it open. Others use Slack because it's what work tools connect to. Here's how they compare for a working team, what each does better, and when neither is quite the right shape.

sections.title: Discord and Slack at a glance

head: Discord
Slack
rows: Free; Nitro is extra for each person
Free plan; paid plans per user
Huddles: 2 people on the free plan, up to 50 on paid plans
Up to 10 apps free, many more on paid plans
Personal accounts, shared with everything else
table.note: From Slack's pricing page and help centre, and Discord's own pages, read in October 2026.

items.title: Talking is the default
items.body: A voice channel is a room people sit in. Drop in, ask, leave: no call to start and nobody to invite.

items.title: Free for the whole team
items.body: Voice, video, screen sharing and full history cost nothing. Nitro adds perks per person, but a team doesn't need it.

items.title: Familiar to a lot of people
items.body: Many developers, designers and students already use it every day, so there's nothing to install or learn.

items.title: Made for work
items.body: Threads, search, workflows and the integrations work tools expect, from calendars to issue trackers.

items.title: The company owns the workspace
items.body: Accounts, retention and access are the company's to manage, and work stays separate from people's personal servers.

items.title: Easier for clients and new hires
items.body: Shared channels with other companies, guest accounts and single sign-on on higher plans.

sections.title: What neither does well
body: Discord shows who's in which voice channel, but not who's at their desk and free for a minute. Slack shows a green dot, which says someone is online, not whether they can talk. In both, starting a conversation means either calling someone out of the blue or typing and waiting.

That gap is what a [virtual office](/virtual-office) fills: everyone has a desk on one floor, sets a status, and walks up to talk, so a team can tell at a glance who's free and step into a room together. Many teams keep Slack or Discord for writing and use an office for talking.

items.title: Discord, for a team that mostly talks
items.body: A small team that lives in voice, is happy with personal accounts and needs few integrations.

items.title: Slack, for a team that mostly writes
items.body: A team that needs search, integrations, client channels and company-owned accounts, and will pay per person for group calls.

items.title: A virtual office beside either
items.body: If the problem is knowing who's free and talking without scheduling, add an office for the day and keep the chat tool you have. Compare [Discord for work](/discord-for-work) and [Slack huddles](/slack-huddles-alternative) with TinyFloor.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor is a private virtual office for small teams: a desk for each person, statuses, walk-up calls, a meeting room, team chat and a whiteboard, in the browser. It's built for work, unlike Discord, and talking is the default, unlike Slack. It's free for up to 3 people and $29 a month for the whole team, and it sits fine next to the chat tool you already use.

faq.q: Is Discord good for work?
faq.a: For a small team that mostly talks, yes: voice channels are free and quick. It's weaker on search, integrations and company-owned accounts, and work sits next to people's personal servers.

faq.q: Is Discord free for teams?
faq.a: Yes. Voice, video, screen sharing and message history are free. Nitro is an optional paid extra for each person.

faq.q: How many people can join a Slack huddle?
faq.a: Two on Slack's free plan. Paid plans allow up to 50, with up to 25 on video.

faq.q: Can we use Discord and Slack together?
faq.a: Some teams do, writing in Slack and talking in Discord, but two tools for one team usually means one of them goes quiet. A virtual office next to your chat tool covers the talking without a second chat.

checkInQuestions.label: Check-in questions

meta.title: 50 Check-In Questions for Meetings: Quick, Deep and Fun
meta.description: 50 check-in questions to open a team meeting, standup or one-on-one: quick one-word rounds, work check-ins, deeper questions, fun ones and questions for remote teams.

checkInQuestions.title: Check-in questions to open any meeting.
checkInQuestions.intro: A check-in is one question everyone answers at the start of a meeting, in a sentence or a word. It gets every voice into the room early, tells you how people are actually doing, and takes two or three minutes. Here are 50 to choose from, grouped by how much time you have and what you want to learn.

items.title: One question, everyone answers
items.body: Go round in a fixed order, or let the last person pick the next. Allow a pass.

items.title: Keep answers short
items.body: A word or a sentence. If something needs more, note it and come back to it after the meeting.

items.title: Match the question to the meeting
items.body: A quick round before a [standup](/virtual-standup), a deeper question before a [retro](/guides/retrospective-ideas) or a [one-on-one](/guides/one-on-one-meeting-questions).

items.title: Answer it yourself first
items.body: The person running the meeting goes first and sets the length and the tone.

sections.title: Quick check-ins (one word or a number)

items.title: One word for how you're arriving today?
items.body: Simple, and surprisingly honest.

items.title: On a scale of 1 to 10, how's your energy?
items.body: Useful for deciding how much to fit into the meeting.

items.title: What's the weather like in your head right now?
items.body: A gentler way to ask how someone is.

items.title: Green, yellow or red for this week?
items.body: A fast read on workload before planning.

items.title: What's one thing on your mind that isn't this meeting?
items.body: Saying it out loud often makes it easier to set aside.

items.title: Coffee, tea or something else today?
items.body: Low stakes, good for a new team.

items.title: Emoji for your week so far?
items.body: Works well typed in the chat at the same time.

items.title: How many hours did you sleep, roughly?
items.body: Only for a team that's comfortable with it.

items.title: What are you looking forward to this week?
items.body: Starts the meeting on something good.

items.title: Focused, scattered or somewhere in between?
items.body: Handy before a working session.

items.title: What's the one thing you most need to finish this week?
items.body: Surfaces priorities without a full status round.

items.title: What's blocking you right now?
items.body: Gets problems into the open early.

items.title: What did you learn since we last met?
items.body: Spreads knowledge across the team.

items.title: What are you waiting on from someone here?
items.body: Turns hidden dependencies into a quick conversation.

items.title: What took longer than you expected last week?
items.body: Good before planning.

items.title: What would make today a good day?
items.body: Gives everyone a small, reachable goal.

items.title: What's one thing you'd drop if you could?
items.body: Shows where the load is too heavy.

items.title: Who helped you this week?
items.body: Builds a habit of noticing each other's help.

items.title: What's something you shipped that you're proud of?
items.body: Wins get named, not just finished.

items.title: What's one question you want answered in this meeting?
items.body: Makes sure the meeting covers what people need.

items.title: What's taking up most of your attention outside work?
items.body: Only answered as far as someone wants.

items.title: When did you last feel really useful at work?
items.body: Good in a one-on-one or a retro.

items.title: What's something you're finding hard right now?
items.body: Needs trust; answer it yourself first.

items.title: What would you change about how we work together?
items.body: An opening for a retro.

items.title: What do you need more of from this team?
items.body: Turns feelings into something the team can act on.

items.title: What's a decision you're still unsure about?
items.body: Invites help without asking for it.

items.title: What are you curious about lately?
items.body: Shows a side of people that work rarely does.

items.title: What would make next month better than this one?
items.body: Good for a monthly meeting.

items.title: What's something you've changed your mind about?
items.body: Models being open to being wrong.

items.title: How are you, really?
items.body: Ask it slowly and wait for the answer.

items.title: What's the best thing you ate this week?
items.body: Everyone has an answer.

items.title: What's on your desk that we can't see?
items.body: Gets people looking around and laughing.

items.title: If today were a film genre, which one?
items.body: A quick, playful read on the week.

items.title: What's a small thing that made you happy recently?
items.body: Ends up being the warmest few minutes of the meeting.

items.title: What song is stuck in your head?
items.body: Optional: play ten seconds of it.

items.title: Which app could you not live without this week?
items.body: Often turns into useful tips.

items.title: What's a skill you'd learn instantly if you could?
items.body: Reveals what people care about.

items.title: Best thing you've watched or read lately?
items.body: Builds a list of recommendations.

items.title: What would your out-of-office message say today?
items.body: Gets creative answers.

items.title: Window seat or aisle?
items.body: Settles nothing and everyone has an opinion.

items.title: What's the view from where you're working today?
items.body: Shows the places behind the video tiles.

items.title: What time is it for you, and what's next after this?
items.body: Makes time zones visible.

items.title: Who did you talk to today, apart from us?

meetingMinutes.title: A meeting minutes template people actually read.
meetingMinutes.intro: Meeting minutes are the short written record of what a meeting decided and who's doing what next. Good minutes are read in a minute and save the next meeting from repeating this one. Here's a template you can copy, what belongs in it, an example, and how to take minutes when the meeting is remote.

sections.title: What minutes are for
body: Minutes aren't a transcript. Nobody reads a word-for-word record, and writing one keeps the note-taker out of the conversation.
Write down what will matter next week: what was decided, what was left open, and who agreed to do what by when. If someone missed the meeting, the minutes should be enough for them to act.

sections.title: A meeting minutes template
body: Copy this into your notes or your team chat at the start of the meeting and fill it in as you go.

head: Section
What to write
rows: Name, date, and who was there
One line: why the meeting happened
Each decision in one sentence, as it was agreed
What, who, and by when, one per line
What wasn't settled, and who will follow up
table.note: Six short sections. If a section is empty, leave it out rather than writing "none".

items.title: Decisions, word for word
items.body: Write the decision the way the group agreed it, so nobody remembers a different version later.

items.title: Actions with a name and a date
items.body: "Look into pricing" gets forgotten. "Sam: three pricing options by Friday" gets done.

items.title: Open questions
items.body: What was raised and not settled, so it doesn't vanish between meetings.

items.title: Who was there
items.body: One line. It tells readers who to ask about what was said.

items.title: Who said what
items.body: Unless it's a formal meeting that needs it, attributing every comment slows the writing and the reading.

items.title: The whole discussion
items.body: One line of context for a decision is enough. The minutes are the outcome, not the debate.

items.title: Opinions about the meeting
items.body: Keep the minutes neutral. Feedback on how the meeting went belongs in a retro.

sections.title: An example
body: Weekly product meeting, 14 October. Ana, Sam, Priya, Tom. Purpose: decide the launch date and the pricing page.

Decisions: the launch moves to Thursday 23 October. The pricing page shows monthly prices only. Actions: Sam, final pricing copy by Monday. Priya, launch email draft by Tuesday. Tom, check the sign-up flow on mobile by Wednesday. Open question: whether to offer a yearly plan later; Ana will bring numbers next week. Next meeting: 21 October.

sections.title: Taking minutes in a remote meeting

items.title: Share the notes on screen
items.body: When everyone sees the minutes being written, mistakes get fixed on the spot and nobody argues about them later.

items.title: Read the actions back
items.body: Spend the last two minutes reading out each action, owner and date. It's the most useful two minutes of the meeting.

items.title: Rotate the note-taker
items.body: The person writing can't lead the discussion. Take turns, and don't always ask the newest or quietest person.

items.title: Post them where the team works
items.body: In the team chat, within the hour, so people who weren't there see them the same day.

items.title: Send the minutes
items.body: The same day, in the team chat or the channel for that project.

items.title: Check the actions
items.body: Start the next meeting by going through last time's actions: done, in progress or stuck.

items.title: Keep them in one place
items.body: A single document or channel per meeting, newest first, so decisions can be found later.

fit.body: TinyFloor is a virtual office for small teams. It doesn't take notes or record meetings for you. It's free for up to 3 people and $29 a month for the whole team.

faq.q: What should meeting minutes include?
faq.a: Who was there, the purpose, the decisions, the actions with an owner and a date, open questions, and when the next meeting is.

faq.q: How do you write meeting minutes quickly?
faq.a: Use a template, write decisions and actions rather than the discussion, and read the actions back at the end so the minutes are finished when the meeting is.

faq.q: Who should take the minutes?
faq.a: Rotate it. The person running the meeting shouldn't also take the notes, and it shouldn't always fall to the same person.

faq.q: What's the difference between an agenda and minutes?
faq.a: The agenda is the plan for the meeting, written before it. The minutes are the record of what it decided, written during and after it.

questionOfTheDay.title: Question of the day for work.
questionOfTheDay.intro: A question of the day is one easy question your team answers every morning: in the team chat, at the start of the standup, or as a poll. It takes a minute, nobody has to prepare, and over a few weeks people learn more about each other than in a year of status meetings. Here are 120 to pick from, grouped by mood, with a few tips for keeping it going.

sections.title: How to run a question of the day

items.title: Pick one place
items.body: A channel in the [team chat](/team-chat) called #question-of-the-day, or the first minute of the [standup](/virtual-standup). The same place every day makes it a habit.

items.title: Post it at the same time
items.body: First thing in the morning for the earliest time zone, so everyone sees it during their day.

items.title: Keep answers short
items.body: A word, a sentence or an emoji. Easy questions get answers; hard ones get silence.

items.title: Rotate who asks
items.body: Hand the question to a different person each week. People start bringing their own, and the questions get better.

items.title: Answer first
items.body: Whoever posts the question answers it straight away. It shows the length and the tone, and nobody has to go first.

faq.q: What is a good question of the day for work?
faq.a: One that anyone can answer in a sentence, says something about the person, and is fine to share at work, like "What's the best thing you've eaten this week?" or "Coffee or tea?".

faq.q: How do you do a question of the day at work?
faq.a: Post one question at the same time every morning in a team chat channel or at the start of the standup, answer it yourself first, and rotate who asks each week.

faq.q: How do you keep a question of the day going?
faq.a: Keep the questions easy, mix fun ones with the occasional work question, and let different people ask. When people start suggesting questions, it runs itself.
